genZNote: Used to be filed under Enterobacter, then genomics said 'actually, that's a Klebsiella' — a good reminder that taxonomy keeps changing under clinicians' feet.

morphology.capsule: Thin capsule (less prominent than K. pneumoniae)
morphology.notes: Unlike most other Klebsiella species, K. aerogenes is motile — historically its classification under Enterobacter reflected this.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil, water, and the human/animal gastrointestinal tract
habitat.hostAssociation: Can be part of normal gut microbiota in small numbers; opportunistic nosocomial pathogen
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Found in soil, sewage, and hospital environments including sinks and equipment

culture.colonyMorphology: Mucoid, lactose-fermenting pink colonies on MacConkey agar

identificationClues: Motile — an unusual feature that distinguishes it from most other Klebsiella species and reflects its former classification as Enterobacter aerogenes
Mucoid, lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar similar to other Enterobacterales
Chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase can be induced, leading to resistance emerging during cephalosporin therapy
Recovered from the same hospital-associated infection sites (urine, blood, respiratory tract, wounds) as other Enterobacterales

clinicalImportance.transmission: Nosocomial — contaminated hospital equipment, hands, and water sources, or endogenous gut flora translocation
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the SPICE/AmpC-producing organisms of concern, since resistance can emerge on therapy even when initial susceptibility testing looks favorable
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Motility is a helpful differentiator from other Klebsiella species when working through an unusual identification

examFacts.importantTest: Motility test; AmpC induction concern with cephalosporin therapy
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Reclassified from Enterobacter to Klebsiella based on genomic data; notably motile unlike most Klebsiella
